advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Handle the (rater_a missing, rater_b valid) case in _final_label instead of falling through to 'unlabeled'.
evidence: 75:    a = row.get("rater_a") if row.get("rater_a") in _VALID else None
82:    if a in _VALID and b is None:  # outside the double-labeled subset — Rater A only
84:    return a, "unlabeled"

adjudicate.py:255 sets row['rater_a']='' on any exception, so a subset row Rater B validly labeled but Rater A failed on becomes a=None,b in _VALID -> falls to 'unlabeled', discarding B's label. README documents exactly one such Rater-A-empty row (runs/README.md:240).
advisory.finding: apply_adjudications._final_label silently DISCARDS a valid Rater-B label when Rater A's label is missing/blank. For a row not in verdicts where a is None but b in _VALID, control falls through both the (a and b) branch and the (a and b is None) branch to return (None, 'unlabeled') — Rater B's committed TP/FP is dropped and the row is treated as having no label.
scenarios: Rater A's LLM call errors/returns empty on a row that is also in Rater B's stratified subset and B produced a valid label.
advisory.suggested_fix: Add a branch: `if a is None and b in _VALID: return b, "single-rater-B"` before the final `return None, "unlabeled"`.

The membership test against them is therefore dead, and a reader may believe verify_s5 distinguishes them.
scenarios: Maintainer reads verify_s5 and assumes the semantic §5.2 classes are computed.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Key member_overrides by (ticket_id, finding_id) rather than bare finding_id to avoid cross-ticket id collisions within a cluster.
evidence: 55:        member_ids = {str(m["finding_id"]) for m in c["members"]}
63:            verdicts[_key(m["ticket_id"], fid)] = overrides.get(fid, cluster_label)
adjudicate.py: "finding_ids can collide across tickets, so key on the pair." (docstring of _key)
cluster_disputes buckets by (source, criterion) only, so a cluster's members can span multiple tickets.
advisory.finding: apply_adjudications member_overrides are keyed by bare finding_id, which cannot disambiguate two members of the same cluster that share a finding_id across different tickets. adjudicate._key explicitly notes finding_ids collide across tickets, and clusters can span tickets, so an override would apply to the wrong (ticket_id,finding_id) member.
scenarios: An operator sets a per-member override in a cluster whose members span two tickets that happen to share a finding_id.

dropped.checklist_item: - [ ] Distinguish a permanent parse failure from an un-attempted row so deterministically-unparseable rows are not re-billed on every run.
evidence: 200:def _needs(row: dict[str, Any], field: str) -> bool:
201:    return row.get(field) not in {"TP", "FP", "ambiguous"}
255:            row["tp_fp"] = row["rater_a"] = ""  # blank on error -> _needs stays True forever
247: comment: "repeated runs converge coverage cheaply (a rate-limited row is retried next run, not re-billed)."
dropped.finding: adjudicate.py re-bills a permanently-unparseable Rater-A row on every full re-run. A blank label ('') fails _needs (not in the valid set), so a row that deterministically yields no parseable label (e.g. all budget spent on thinking, no text block) is retried and re-billed on every run and never converges, contradicting the 'converge coverage cheaply / not re-billed' design note.
scenarios: A hard finding on which the model, at temperature 0, always emits only thinking with no text block; every subsequent `python adjudicate.py` re-attempts and re-bills it.

dropped.finding: The reviewed-ticket population size is documented with three inconsistent numbers across the change: the commit message says outcome_corpus.jsonl has '628 rows, one per reviewed ticket'; mine_outcome_corpus.py's docstring says the '§5.1 population, ~527'; and the same docstring later says '140 of 631 reviewed tickets (22%)'. A reader cannot tell whether the reviewed population is 527, 628, or 631, or reconcile 'one row per reviewed ticket' with 628 rows.
scenarios: A future maintainer or auditor tries to reconcile the frozen corpus row count against the documented population and finds three different figures.
